title: HashMap collision handling — chaining → treeify at threshold 8
shortTitle: HashMap collision handling — chaining → treeify at threshold 8

s1_definition.profdef: When two keys have the same bucket index (`hash & (capacity-1)`), a collision occurs. HashMap resolves collisions by **chaining** — storing multiple entries in the same bucket as a linked list. Java 8+: when a bucket's chain reaches **8 nodes** (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) AND the table has **≥64 buckets**, the chain converts to a Red-Black tree → lookup changes from O(n) to O(log n). When the tree shrinks to ≤6 nodes (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it converts back to a linked list.
s1_definition.oneliner: Collision → linked list chain. ≥8 nodes + ≥64 buckets → Red-Black tree (O(log n)). ≤6 nodes → back to linked list.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When two keys have the same bucket index (`hash & (capacity-1)`), a collision occurs. HashMap resolves collisions by **chaining** — storing multiple entries in the same bucket as a linked list. Java 8+: when a bucket's chain reaches **8 nodes** (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) AND the table has **≥64 buckets**, the chain converts to a Red-Black tree → lookup changes from O(n) to O(log n). When the tree shrinks to ≤6 nodes (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it converts back to a linked list.

**One line to remember:** Collision → linked list chain. ≥8 nodes + ≥64 buckets → Red-Black tree (O(log n)). ≤6 nodes → back to linked list.

sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, the engineering team hit a real problem that maps directly onto HashMap collision handling and treeification. Rajesh (account SAV2001, a software engineer with a savings balance of 1,000,000 rupees) and Priya (account CUR3001, a property owner with a current balance of 250,000 rupees) both run operations that stress the system's collection handling, and the wrong data-structure choice here caused slow lookups, lost entries, or incorrect ordering in production reports.

The mini-project below reproduces that banking scenario and shows exactly how HashMap collision handling and treeification solves it correctly, using BigDecimal for every money value and the same Account model with debit and credit behaviour.
sections.s5_journey:
The input is many keys that hash into the same bucket of a HashMap.

**Step 1.** The first colliding key for Rajesh's region is stored as a linked-list node in the bucket.

**Step 2.** Each additional colliding key is chained onto that bucket's linked list, so lookups in that bucket walk the chain in O(n).

**Step 3.** Once the chain length reaches the treeify threshold of 8 (with table capacity at least 64), the bucket converts to a Red-Black tree, dropping worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n).
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Input: Rajesh SAV2001 (Rs.1,000,000), Priya CUR3001 (Rs.250,000)
    │
    ▼
  Service layer (applies HashMap collision handling and treeification)
    │  loads accounts into the collection
    │  performs the operation (add / lookup / order / dedup)
    ▼
  Collection state changes
    │  SAV2001 and CUR3001 processed with BigDecimal amounts
    ▼
  Output: correct result returned to the caller
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  Account Lookup Store (Bank)
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ HashMap<String,Account> table │
  └───────────────┬──────────────┘
    collision → same bucket index
                 ▼
   bucket[i]: node → node → node ...   (linked list)
         chain ≥ 8  AND  table ≥ 64 buckets
                 ▼
   bucket[i]: Red-Black Tree  (O(n) → O(log n))
         chain ≤ 6  →  back to linked list
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Collisions are resolved by chaining (linked list → tree at 8). Good hashCode() minimizes collisions. Java 8's treeification is a SAFETY NET, not a feature to rely on — fix your hashCode() instead.
